claim: Pheochromocytomas (PCCs) are rare neuroendocrine tumors that originate from chromaffin cells in the adrenal gland.
source: Pheochromocytomas (PCCs) are rare neuroendocrine tumors that originate from chromaffin cells in the adrenal gland (Fishbein et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Nölting et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Fishbein et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Nölting et al., 2022).

claim: PCCs display a remarkable diversity of driver alterations, including germline and somatic mutations as well as somatic fusion genes.
source: PCCs have been shown to display a remarkable diversity of driver alterations, including germline and somatic mutations as well as somatic fusion genes (Favier et al., 2015; Pillai et al., 2017; Toledo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Favier et al., 2015; Pillai et al., 2017; Toledo et al., 2017).

claim: 50~60% of PCCs fail to be classified using the TCGA molecular taxonomy system.
source: However, 50~60% of PCCs fail to be classified using this system (Lenders et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Lenders et al., 2014).

claim: Since 2017, all PCCs are regarded as malignant tumors with metastatic potential according to the WHO pathological classification.
source: since 2017, all PCCs are regarded as malignant tumors with metastatic potential according to the WHO pathological classification (Lam, 2017; Mete et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Lam, 2017; Mete et al., 2022).

claim: The intra-tumoral heterogeneity was less extensive than the inter-individual heterogeneity of PCCs.
source: We found that intra-tumoral heterogeneity was less extensive than the inter-individual heterogeneity of PCCs.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data analysis showing correlation patterns among specimens.

claim: Unclassified PCC patients were divided into two types: metabolism-type (marked by NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2) and kinase-type (marked by RET and PNMT).
source: Further, the unclassified PCC patients were divided into two types, metabolism-type (marked by NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2) and kinase-type (marked by RET and PNMT), validated by immunohistochemical staining.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data, CNV analysis, and immunohistochemical staining validation.

claim: Metabolism-type PCC cells display phenotype of consistently active metabolism and increased metastasis potential.
source: Trajectory analysis of tumor evolution revealed that metabolism-type PCC cells display phenotype of consistently active metabolism and increased metastasis potential
evidence: Supported by trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data showing gene expression patterns over pseudotime.

claim: Kinase-type PCC cells showed decreased epinephrine synthesis and neuron-like phenotypes.
source: while kinase-type PCC cells showed decreased epinephrine synthesis and neuron-like phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data showing gene expression patterns over pseudotime.

claim: The annexin pathway is activated in metabolism-type PCCs.
source: Cell-cell communication analysis showed activation of the annexin pathway and a strong inflammation reaction in metabolism-type PCCs
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Metabolism-type PCCs show a strong inflammation reaction.
source: Cell-cell communication analysis showed activation of the annexin pathway and a strong inflammation reaction in metabolism-type PCCs
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis and GSEA enrichment analysis.

claim: FGF signaling is activated in the kinase-type PCC.
source: and activation of FGF signaling in the kinase-type PCC.
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs lack CD8+ T cell infiltration.
source: Although multispectral immunofluorescence staining showed a lack of CD8+ T cell infiltration in both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs
evidence: Supported by multispectral immunofluorescence staining data.

claim: Only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules.
source: only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules that possibly regulated by RET
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data and immunohistochemistry staining.

claim: HLA-I downregulation in kinase-type PCCs is possibly regulated by RET.
source: only the kinase-type PCC exhibited downregulation of HLA-I molecules that possibly regulated by RET
evidence: Inferred from the co-occurrence of RET expression and HLA-I downregulation, and supported by prior literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I.

claim: Kinase-type PCCs have potential for combined therapy with kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy.
source: suggesting the potential of combined therapy with kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy for kinase-type PCCs
evidence: Speculative claim based on the observed HLA-I downregulation and RET expression patterns.

claim: The application of immunotherapy to metabolism-type PCCs is likely unsuitable.
source: in contrast, the application of immunotherapy to metabolism-type PCCs (with antigen presentation ability) is likely unsuitable.
evidence: Speculative claim based on the lack of CD8+ T cell infiltration despite antigen presentation ability.

claim: 133,894 individual cells were retained after quality control filtering.
source: After quality control filtering to remove cells with low gene detection and high mitochondrial gene coverage, we retained 133,894 individual cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–2C).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data processing and quality control metrics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–2C.

claim: 13 cell types were identified in the PCC microenvironment including adrenal cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, T cells, natural killer cells, proliferating cells, plasma cells, B cells, mast cells, and sustentacular cells.
source: We classified the 67 detected clusters into 13 cell types according to their expression profiles for recognized marker genes and Spearman correlation analysis between clusters: the classified cell types included adrenal cells (marked by DLK1 and RBP1), endothelial cells (marked by PECAM1 and VWF), fibroblasts (marked by THY1 and PLAC9), smooth muscle cells (marked by ACTA2 and TAGLN), monocytes/macrophages (marked by CD14 and CD163), neutrophils (marked by S100A8 and S100A9), T cells (marked by IL7R and CD3D), natural killer cells (NKs, marked by KLRD1 and GNLY), proliferating cells (marked by TOP2A and MKI67), plasma cells (marked by XBP1 and IGKC), B cells (marked by MS4A1 and CD79A), mast cells (marked by KIT and TPSB2), and sustentacular cells (marked by S100B and CRYAB) (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by marker gene expression analysis and visualization in Figures 1C, 1D, and supplementary figures.

claim: The PASS scores of 11 collected PCC tissues ranged from 2 to 9.
source: The PASS scores of 11 collected PCC tissues ranged from 2 to 9, showing obvious heterogeneity among the examined intra-tumoral sites and inter-individual comparisons for the 5 PCC patients (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by PASS scoring data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: P4 showed low correlation with the other three sporadic PCCs patients (P1-P3).
source: The inter-individual correlation analysis indicated that P4 showed low correlation with the other three sporadic PCCs patients (P1-P3) (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: P4 had a significantly elevated proportion of adrenal cells (77%) compared to P1-P3 (16-36%).
source: and further analysis of cell type fractions showed a significantly elevated proportion of adrenal cells (77%) in P4; the adrenal cells comprised between 16 and 36% of the total cells in the P1-P3 specimens (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: P5 had a higher proportion of endothelial cells (35%) compared to P1-P4 (3–10%).
source: reflecting a higher proportion of endothelial cells in P5 (35%) as compared to P1-P4 (3–10%) (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: VHL syndrome is associated with vascular endothelial hyperplasia.
source: Consistent with the reported vascular endothelial hyperplasia phenotype in VHL syndrome (Vortmeyer et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Vortmeyer et al., 2013).

claim: CopyKAT algorithm distinguishes PCC cells from normal chromaffin cells based on genomic copy number variants.
source: The copy number karyotyping of aneuploid tumors (CopyKAT) algorithm (Gao et al., 2021) was applied, which estimates genomic copy number variants (CNVs) from scRNA-seq data by employing an integrative Bayesian segmentation approach to distinguish PCC cells from normal chromaffin cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to the CopyKAT method (Gao et al., 2021) and its application to the scRNA-seq data.

claim: Inferred aneuploid tumor cells highly expressed Chromogranin B (CHGB), which is a marker of PCC cells.
source: Consistently, the inferred aneuploid tumor cells highly expressed Chromogranin B (CHGB), which is a marker of PCC cells (Wiedenmann et al., 1988; Winkler and Fischer-Colbrie, 1992; Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B and C, and citations to prior literature (Wiedenmann et al., 1988; Winkler and Fischer-Colbrie, 1992).

claim: Two CNV patterns were identified among the inferred aneuploid tumor cells, with distinctions evident in chromosomes 3, 11, and 17.
source: We noticed two CNV patterns among the inferred aneuploid tumor cells, with the distinction evident in chromosomes 3, 11, and 17 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells in inferred tumor cluster A exhibited high expression of NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2.
source: We observed that cells in inferred tumor cluster A exhibited high expression of NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis of tumor clusters.

claim: Cells in inferred tumor cluster B expressed high levels of PNMT and RET.
source: while cells in inferred tumor cluster B expressed high levels of PNMT and RET (Figure 3D and E)
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: PNMT is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine.
source: PNMT is known as an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of norepinephrine to epinephrine
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about PNMT function.

claim: RET is a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family.
source: and that RET is a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about RET.

claim: NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 function in the oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis pathways.
source: while NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 respectively function in the oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis pathways (Drilon et al., 2018; Mahmoodi et al., 2020; Sinkler et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drilon et al., 2018; Mahmoodi et al., 2020; Sinkler et al., 2017).

claim: Tumor cluster A DEGs showed functional enrichment for terms including generation of metabolites and energy, response to oxygen levels, response to hypoxia, and ATP metabolic process.
source: the tumor cluster A DEGs showed functional enrichment for terms including generation of metabolites and energy, response to oxygen levels, response to hypoxia, and ATP metabolic process and some notably upregulated genes of tumor cluster A included known energy metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, COX4I2, RGS4, and AQP1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tumor cluster B DEGs showed enrichment for terms including cytoplasmic translation, neuron projection development, axon development, and cell growth.
source: For tumor cluster B, the GO analysis showed enrichment for terms including cytoplasmic translation, neuron projection development, axon development, and cell growth, and there was obvious upregulation of PNMT, RET, and genes encoding other kinases known to function in proliferation, as well as genes that participate in the regulation of neuroendocrine functions (e.g. CALM1, PENK, and NPY; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Immunocytochemistry staining showed strong accumulation of PNMT and RET in P4.
source: Notably, immunocytochemistry staining of serial tumor sections showed strong accumulation of PNMT and RET in P4
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 accumulation was characteristic for the P1-P3 and P5 sections.
source: while NDUFA4L2 and COX4I2 accumulation was characteristic for the P1-P3 and P5 sections, providing protein-level evidence to validate the differential trends detected from the scRNA-seq results (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: P4 exhibited relatively higher blood pressures and plasma levels of 3-methoxytyramine and normetanephrine compared to P1-P3 and P5.
source: When considering clinical information from five PCC patients, including tumor size, signs, symptoms and laboratory tests, we observed that P4 exhibited relatively higher blood pressures and the plasma levels of 3-methoxytyramine and normetanephrine compared to P1-P3 and P5 (Supplementary file 1c)
evidence: Supported by clinical data in Supplementary file 1c.

claim: Late up-regulated genes in metabolism-type PCCs include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion.
source: Late up-regulated genes include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion, which highly expressed in subcluster 2 (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C and established knowledge about S100A4 and TAGLN functions.

claim: Metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, ATP5MG, NDUFB4, and COX17 were highly expressed at early stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
source: Metabolism-related genes such as NDUFA4L2, ATP5MG, NDUFB4, and COX17 were highly expressed at early stage, while SOD3 and COX7A1 were up-regulated at the late stage (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 is highly expressed at early stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
source: We also found the high expression of tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 at early stage and subsequent up-regulation of the oncogene JUNB (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Oncogene JUNB is up-regulated at late stage in metabolism-type PCCs.
source: We also found the high expression of tumor suppressor gene SPINT2 at early stage and subsequent up-regulation of the oncogene JUNB (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CALM1 and CALM2 are highly expressed early in kinase-type PCC cells.
source: Further analysis of DEGs in the pseudotime trajectory showed early high expression of CALM1 and CALM2 in the subcluster 1, and late up-regulation of RET in the subcluster 2 (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: RET is up-regulated late in kinase-type PCC cells.
source: Further analysis of DEGs in the pseudotime trajectory showed early high expression of CALM1 and CALM2 in the subcluster 1, and late up-regulation of RET in the subcluster 2 (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PNMT is expressed early in kinase-type PCC cells.
source: We also noticed the early expression of PNMT, while neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 were up-regulated later in the pseudotime trajectory (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 are up-regulated later in kinase-type PCC cells.
source: We also noticed the early expression of PNMT, while neuron-specific genes such as MAP2, MAP1B, L1CAM, and CNTN1 were up-regulated later in the pseudotime trajectory (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PCC cells with high expression of RET exhibit neuron-like phenotypes.
source: suggesting the decrease of epinephrine synthesis and the appearance of neuron-like phenotypes during tumor evolution, consistent with previously reported neuron-like phenotypes in PCC cells with high expression of RET (Califano et al., 1995; Powers et al., 2003; Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Califano et al., 1995; Powers et al., 2003; Powers et al., 2009).

claim: ANXA1-FPR1 pair is the major participant in the annexin signaling pathway in metabolism-type PCCs.
source: Further analysis of participated ligand-receptors showed major participation of ANXA1-FPR1 pair in the annexin signaling pathway (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ANXA1 and FPR1 are highly co-expressed in neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages.
source: and high co-expression of ANXA1 and FPR1 in neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The annexin signaling pathway is activated under a strong inflammatory reaction.
source: It has been reported that the annexin signaling pathway is known to be activated under a strong inflammatory reaction (Gastardelo et al., 2014; Gavins et al., 2003; Gerke and Moss, 2002; Hayhoe et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Gastardelo et al., 2014; Gavins et al., 2003; Gerke and Moss, 2002; Hayhoe et al., 2006).

claim: Metabolism-type PCCs have a higher proportion of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages compared with kinase-type.
source: Combined with our findings of a higher proportion of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages in metabolism-type as compared with kinase-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inflammatory response signaling pathway showed enrichment in metabolism-type PCCs compared with kinase-type PCC.
source: As expected, the inflammatory response signaling pathway showed enrichment in metabolism-type PCCs as compared with that in kinase-type PCC (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: VEGF signaling pathway is activated in P5 (VHL patient).
source: We noticed the activation of VEGF signaling pathway in P5 (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs are major contributors to VEGF signaling pathway in P5.
source: and major contribution of PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs to VEGF signaling pathway (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: VEGFA and VEGFR1 are highly expressed in tumor cells in P5.
source: Specifically, VEGFA and VEGFR1 were highly expressed in tumor cells, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 in endothelial cells, and PLGF in fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 6G)
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: FGF1-FGFR1 is the major participant in the FGF pathway in kinase-type PCC.
source: and identified the activation of FGF signaling network (Figure 6H) and major involvement of FGF1-FGFR1 in the FGF pathway (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6H and 6I.

claim: Smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1 in kinase-type PCC.
source: The smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1, while tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 in kinase-type PCC.
source: The smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and B cells exhibited high expression of FGF1, while tumor cells, smooth muscle cells, T cells, and B cells highly expressed FGFR1 (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6J.

claim: FGF1-FGFR1 pair regulates tumor cell proliferation.
source: The analyses suggested the cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells through the FGF1-FGFR1 pair, which regulated the tumor cell proliferation (Katoh, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Katoh, 2016).

claim: Kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors.
source: These results indicate that kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors, which have been shown to exert inhibitory effects on tumor proliferation (Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative claim based on FGF signaling activation and citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2012).

claim: There is apparent crosstalk between tumor cells and T cells in metabolism-type patients.
source: Visualization of inter-cellular communication showed apparent crosstalk between tumor cells and T cells in metabolism-type patients
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There is a lack of apparent communication between tumor cells and T cells in the kinase-type patient.
source: while we were surprised to find a lack of apparent communication between tumor cells and T cells in the kinase-type patient (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Kinase-type PCC cells could evade immune surveillance of T cells.
source: These results suggested that kinase-type PCC cells could evade immune surveillance of T cells and further indicated the immune escape potential of kinase-type PCCs.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of communication between tumor cells and T cells.

claim: HLA-I surface level represents the antigen-presenting abilities of tumor cells.
source: Considering leukocyte antigen-class I (HLA-I) surface level is known to represent the antigen-presenting abilities of tumor cells (Brea et al., 2016; Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Brea et al., 2016; Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2019).

claim: The expression levels of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C were significantly lower in kinase-type PCC cells than in metabolism-type PCC cells.
source: the expression levels of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C were significantly lower in kinase-type PCC cells than in metabolism-type PCC cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Immunohistochemistry staining showed lower expression of HLA-A in P4 compared to other patients.
source: Consistently, immunohistochemistry staining of serial sections of tumor tissues showed lower expression of HLA-A in P4 as compared to that in other patients (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Eight immune cell types were identified including central memory CD4+ T cells, effector memory CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer T cells, natural killer cells, B cells, M1 macrophages, and M2 macrophages.
source: We additionally assessed the immune microenvironment of PCCs by subclustering immunotherapy-related immune cells and identified eight clusters including central memory CD4+ T cells (CD4+ TCM, marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, CCR7, and IL7R), effector memory CD4+ T cells (CD4+ TEM, marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD4, and IL7R), CD8+ T cells (marked by CD3D, CD3E, CD3G, CD8A and CD8B), natural killer T cells (NKTs, marked by CD3E, KLRD1 and GNLY), natural killer cells (NKs, marked by KLRD1 and GNLY), B cells (marked by MS4A1 and CD79A), M1 macrophages (marked by CD68), and M2 macrophages (marked by CD68 and CD163) (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Supported by marker gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: The proportion of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages increased in tumor tissues compared with adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues.
source: Further analysis of immune cell type composition in metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs showed an increase in the proportion of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages in tumor tissues as compared with that in adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues
evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The proportion of M2 macrophages decreased in tumor tissues compared with adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues.
source: while the proportion of M2 macrophages in adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues decreased as compared with that in tumor tissues (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CD8+ T cells play an essential role in anti-tumor immunity by recognizing tumor antigens displayed on the surface of tumor cells by HLA-I molecules.
source: In particular, the CD8+ T cells play an essential role in anti-tumor immunity; these cells can recognize tumor antigens displayed on the surface of tumor cells by HLA-I molecules (Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Jhunjhunwala et al., 2021).

claim: CD8+ T cells were rare and only present in tumor stroma of P1-P5.
source: We observed that CD8+ T cells, as well as CD4+ T cells, M1 macrophages, and M2 macrophages were rare (and were only present in tumor stroma of P1-P5), indicating apparent immune escape in both metabolism-type and kinase-type PCCs (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by multispectral immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Kinases such as RET, ALK, and MEK have negative regulatory effects on HLA-I expression on tumor cells.
source: Combined with previously reported negative regulatory effects of kinases (such as RET, ALK, and MEK) on HLA-I expression on tumor cells (Brea et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Brea et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2019).

claim: The possible reason for inability in recruiting CD8+ T cells of kinase-type PCCs is the down-regulation of HLA-I in tumor cells regulated by RET.
source: we speculate that the possible reason for inability in recruiting CD8+ T cells of kinase-type PCCs is the down-regulation of HLA-I in tumor cells regulated by RET
evidence: Speculative claim based on observed HLA-I downregulation and prior literature on kinase regulation of HLA-I.

claim: RET inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with RET mutation.
source: Recently, RET inhibitors have been approved for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with RET mutation (Drilon et al., 2020; Griesinger et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Drilon et al., 2020; Griesinger et al., 2022).

claim: 40~50% of PCCs have been classified into a certain molecular pathway (pseudohypoxia, kinase, or Wnt).
source: According to the results of genomics research in recent years, 40~50% of PCCs have been classified into a certain molecular pathway (pseudohypoxia, kinase, or Wnt), but the remaining 50–60% are still unclassified (Crona et al., 2017; Lenders et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Crona et al., 2017; Lenders et al., 2014).

claim: Isotope therapies can only relieve the clinical symptoms in 50% of patients without reducing tumor size.
source: Isotope therapies can only relieve the clinical symptoms in 50% of patients (without reducing tumor size; Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Roman-Gonzalez and Jimenez, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Roman-Gonzalez and Jimenez, 2017).

claim: Most chemotherapies and targeted therapies exhibit low remission rates and severe side effects in clinical studies for PCCs.
source: while most chemotherapies and targeted therapies exhibit low remission rates and severe side effects in clinical studies (Druce et al., 2009; Hamidi, 2019; O'Kane et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Druce et al., 2009; Hamidi, 2019; O'Kane et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2012).

claim: One clinical trial investigating ICIs for metastatic PCCs showed 43% non-progression rate (NPR) and 0% overall response rate (ORR) in seven PCC patients.
source: Currently, there are only two clinical trials investigating the efficacy of ICIs for the treatment of metastatic PCCs: one is still in the recruitment stage, and the other showed 43% non-progression rate (NPR) and 0% overall response rate (ORR) in seven PCC patients (Dai et al., 2020; Jimenez et al., 2022; Naing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Dai et al., 2020; Jimenez et al., 2022; Naing et al., 2020).

claim: The PASS scoring system is weighted for histologic features and has been used to separate tumors with potential for biologically aggressive behavior (PASS ≥ 4) from tumors with benign lesion (PASS < 4).
source: A scoring system—the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS)—is weighted for histologic features and has been used to separate tumors with a potential for a biologically aggressive behavior (PASS > or = 4) from tumors with benign lesion (PASS < 4) (Thompson, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Thompson, 2002).

claim: The utility of PASS scoring system is restricted due to observer variation and nonrepeatability.
source: Although the PASS scoring system was proposed as a tool for discriminating potentially metastasis PCCs from benign ones, its utility is somewhat restricted due to observer variation and nonrepeatability (Agarwal et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 2014; Thompson, 2002; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Agarwal et al., 2010; Kimura et al., 2014; Thompson, 2002; Wu et al., 2009).

claim: Whole exome sequencing of sporadic PCC tumor tissues detected somatic mutations in JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, and MST1.
source: Four of these patients (P1-P4) suffered from sporadic PCCs: whole exome sequencing (WES) of these tumor tissues detected somatic mutations as compared with their adjacent normal adrenal medullary tissues, including in JAK2, ARHGEF39, KMT2D, and MST1 (Supplementary file 1a)
evidence: Supported by WES data in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: P5 had a germline missense mutation in VHL.
source: The cohort also included 1 hereditary PCC patient (P5) with Type 2 Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, with a germline missense mutation in VHL (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by WES data in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: PCC cells show typical cell arrangement (small alveoli surrounded by fibro-vascular stroma) and characteristic shapes (polygonal or fusiform cells).
source: The morphology of PCC cells was assessed through hematoxylin-eosin-stained tumor tissues, showing the typical cell arrangement (small alveoli surrounded by fibro-vascular stroma) and characteristic shapes (polygonal or fusiform cells) of PCCs (Lupşan et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior literature (Lupşan et al., 2016).

claim: Immunocytochemistry staining showed robust expression of Chromogranin A (CGA) in PCC tumor tissues.
source: Meanwhile, immunocytochemistry staining showed robust expression of Chromogranin A (CGA) in these tumor tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inferred diploid normal cells expressing high levels of CYP17A1 and HSD3B2 were defined as adrenocortical cells.
source: The inferred diploid normal cells expressing high levels of CYP17A1 and HSD3B2 were defined as adrenocortical cells (Kubota-Nakayama et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis and citation to prior literature (Kubota-Nakayama et al., 2016).

claim: Inferred diploid normal cells showing low CHGB expression were defined as normal chromaffin cells.
source: while the inferred diploid normal cells showing low CHGB expression were defined as normal chromaffin cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: A cluster of inferred diploid normal cells with high expression of VWF was found in the VHL patient (P5).
source: We also found a cluster of inferred diploid normal cells with high expression of VWF (a marker for vascular endothelial cells) in the VHL patient (P5) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Metabolism-type PCCs correspond to the pseudo-hypoxic type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
source: These results support that the previously unclassified PCCs can be classified as metabolism-type or kinase-type based on transcriptional programs, with these types partially corresponding to the pseudo-hypoxic type and kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
evidence: Inferred from the molecular characteristics and comparison with TCGA classification.

claim: Kinase-type PCCs correspond to the kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
source: These results support that the previously unclassified PCCs can be classified as metabolism-type or kinase-type based on transcriptional programs, with these types partially corresponding to the pseudo-hypoxic type and kinase-signaling type of PCCs from the TCGA classification.
evidence: Inferred from the molecular characteristics and comparison with TCGA classification.

claim: Kinase-signaling PCCs by TCGA classification include germline and somatic mutations in RET and are uniquely able to secrete epinephrine owing to their high expression of PNMT.
source: Consistently, kinase-signaling PCCs by TCGA classification include germline and somatic mutations in RET, and are uniquely able to secrete epinephrine, owing to their high expression of PNMT
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about TCGA classification of PCCs.

claim: P5 displays reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism caused by VHL mutation and subsequent HIF dysregulation.
source: P5 could also be classified into the metabolism-type we defined, which is known to display reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism caused by VHL mutation and subsequent HIF dysregulation (Chappell et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Chappell et al., 2019).

claim: Subcluster 2 of metabolism-type PCCs has higher metastasis potential compared with subcluster 1.
source: Late up-regulated genes include S100A4 and TAGLN that promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell invasion, which highly expressed in subcluster 2 (Figure 5C), suggesting the higher metastasis potential of subcluster 2 as compared with subcluster 1.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of metastasis-promoting genes in subcluster 2.

claim: The major clone in kinase-type PCCs has changed from subcluster 1 to subcluster 2 along the trajectory.
source: We then clustered kinase-type PCC cells into two subclusters and found that the major clone has been changed from subcluster 1–2 along the trajectory (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: VEGF pathway activation is consistent with vascular endothelial hyperplasia caused by VHL mutation in VHL syndrome.
source: The observed activation of VEGF pathway is consistent with the vascular endothelial hyperplasia caused by VHL mutation in VHL syndrome (Vortmeyer et al., 2013) and the elevated proportion of endothelial cells in this patient (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Vortmeyer et al., 2013) and cell type composition data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PLGF-VEGFR1, VEGFA-VEGFR1 and VEGFA-VEGFR2 pairs mediate tumor angiogenesis and metastasis in P5.
source: Specifically, VEGFA and VEGFR1 were highly expressed in tumor cells, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 in endothelial cells, and PLGF in fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, respectively (Figure 6G), suggesting the crosstalk between tumor cells and fibroblasts or endothelial cells in tumor microenvironment through these ligand-receptor pairs, which mediated in the tumor angiogenesis and metastasis.
evidence: Inferred from the expression patterns of ligands and receptors and established knowledge about VEGF pathway function.

claim: FGF1-FGFR1 pair regulates tumor cell proliferation through cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells.
source: The analyses suggested the cell-cell communication among tumor cells, stroma cells, and immune cells through the FGF1-FGFR1 pair, which regulated the tumor cell proliferation (Katoh, 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the expression patterns of FGF1 and FGFR1 and supported by citation to prior literature (Katoh, 2016).

claim: FGFR inhibitors exert inhibitory effects on tumor proliferation.
source: These results indicate that kinase-type PCCs may benefit from FGFR inhibitors, which have been shown to exert inhibitory effects on tumor proliferation (Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2012).

claim: The mechanism of immune escape in metabolism-type PCCs needs to be further explored.
source: while the mechanism of immune escape in metabolism-type PCCs (with antigen presentation ability) needs to be further explored.
evidence: Acknowledged gap in understanding based on the observed immune escape despite antigen presentation ability.

claim: RET inhibitors may enhance the antigen presentation ability of tumor cells in kinase-type PCCs.
source: For kinase-type PCCs, whether RET inhibitors can enhance the antigen presentation ability of tumor cells, and further provide chance for combination of kinase-targeted therapy and immunotherapy, needs to be verified by follow-up research.
evidence: Speculative claim requiring future verification.

claim: The study included only one patient with a VHL germline mutation.
source: Despite the patient cohort in our study including a hereditary PCC patient, only one patient with a VHL germline mutation was included; other types of hereditary PCCs with germline mutations (for example in SDHx and FH) were not included.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.

claim: The specimens were all from primary tumors, while no metastatic tumors were included.
source: In addition, the specimens were all from primary tumors, while no metastatic tumors were included.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.

claim: The number of sporadic cases was limited, mainly caused by the low incidence of PCCs.
source: The number of sporadic cases was also limited, mainly caused by the low incidence of PCCs.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study.
